title: Dosing a nonlinear drug such as phenytoin

segs.text: Module eight, objective four. Estimating the dose of a nonlinear drug such as phenytoin. The dose here is a dose rate, R, an amount per unit of time such as milligrams per day. C s s is the steady state concentration, the level once dosing and elimination balance. The patient's V max and K M are known, given or found as in objective three. Phenytoin is dosed with care because it is nonlinear and has a narrow therapeutic window, the range between the minimum effective and the minimum toxic level. She said, The range for phenytoin, I think, is ten to twenty milligrams per liter.

card.m: R: dose rate, amount per time (mg/day, mg/kg/day)
V<sub>max</sub>, K<sub>M</sub>: given, or from objective 3

segs.text: At steady state the drug going in each day equals the drug eliminated each day, so R equals the elimination rate at that level. The elimination rate rises with the level but never past V max, so a higher target level needs a higher R, and R must stay below V max. At a daily dose at or above V max, elimination never catches up, because the elimination rate stays below V max at every level, so the level keeps rising and no steady state is reached. Close to V max, a small rise in R gives a large rise in C s s. Steady state takes two to three weeks for such a drug, not three to five half lives.

card.m: steady state: rate in = rate out, so R = elimination rate
R near V<sub>max</sub>: small R ↑ → large C<sub>ss</sub> ↑

segs.text: The dose rate equation says this: R equals V max times C s s, divided by K M plus C s s. C s s on the top raises R, and C s s on the bottom, added to K M, keeps R below V max however high the target. The milligrams per liter on the top and the bottom cancel, so R comes out in the units of V max. When V max is per kilogram, R comes out per kilogram, and the weight then gives the patient's dose.

card.m: {{frac:(mg/day)(mg/L)|mg/L}} = mg/day: R in the units of V<sub>max</sub>
V<sub>max</sub> per kg → R per kg → × weight

segs.text: Turned around, the same equation gives the level a chosen dose rate will produce: C s s equals R times K M, divided by V max minus R. She worked this on the board from the R equation; it is not on the equation sheet. R is on the top and is also subtracted from V max on the bottom, so as R approaches V max the bottom shrinks and C s s climbs steeply. In her slide example, six milligrams per kilogram per day gave ten milligrams per liter, and eight gave twenty, not the thirteen a linear drug would give.

card.m: R(K<sub>M</sub> + C<sub>ss</sub>) = V<sub>max</sub>C<sub>ss</sub> → RK<sub>M</sub> = C<sub>ss</sub>(V<sub>max</sub> − R)
R → V<sub>max</sub>: V<sub>max</sub> − R → 0, C<sub>ss</sub> climbs

segs.text: Her first slide example asks the daily dose rate for an average level of twenty four milligrams per liter in a sixty five kilogram patient, with K M five milligrams per liter and V max eight milligrams per kilogram per day. A target level is given, so the R equation answers it. R is six point six two milligrams per kilogram per day, and four hundred thirty milligrams per day for this patient. The target is almost five times K M, so R is already most of V max, about eighty three percent of it.

card.m: K<sub>M</sub> 5 mg/L, V<sub>max</sub> 8 mg/kg/day; target C<sub>ss</sub> 24 mg/L; 65 kg

segs.text: The per kilogram rate is not the answer for a patient. She said, And if I'm your patient, please don't tell me six point six two milligrams per kilogram per day. Tell me how many, tell me what I need. A per kilogram V max needs the weight at the end; a per day V max does not, and the weight then serves only the volume of distribution. An amount with no time is not a dose rate either. She said, I don't wanna just see one thousand milligrams.

card.m: ✗ per-kg rate left for a patient
V<sub>max</sub> per kg: × weight at the end; per day: weight only for V<sub>D</sub>

segs.text: Her second slide example continues objective three: with K M ten milligrams per liter and V max twelve milligrams per kilogram per day, the dose rate for fifteen milligrams per liter in the seventy two kilogram patient. R is seven point two milligrams per kilogram per day, or five hundred eighteen point four milligrams per day, which she rounded to five hundred twenty on her slide. A check: fifteen lies between her two measured levels, ten and twenty, so R must lie between their dose rates, six and eight, and it does.

card.m: K<sub>M</sub> 10 mg/L, V<sub>max</sub> 12 mg/kg/day; target 15 mg/L; 72 kg

segs.text: Her Solutions one uses the K M of five point nine one milligrams per liter and the V max of six hundred forty seven point eight three milligrams per day from objective three. First, the dose for fifteen milligrams per liter, from the R equation: four hundred sixty four point seven three milligrams per day, which she gave as four hundred sixty five. The weight is not needed, because V max is per day. Then the level on four hundred fifty milligrams daily, from the turned around equation because the dose is now fixed: thirteen point four four milligrams per liter, written thirteen point five on her sheet.

So four hundred fifty milligrams per day is about ninety seven percent of four hundred sixty five, yet the level is thirteen point five instead of fifteen, a tenth lower. Near saturation, the level changes by a larger fraction than the dose, whether the dose goes up or down. That is why levels are measured and the dose adjusted for the individual patient.

card.m: near V<sub>max</sub>: C<sub>ss</sub> changes by a larger fraction than R

segs.text: How she tests it. Most sheets ask a daily dose for fifteen milligrams per liter at steady state, and some then ask the level at another dose, such as eleven point five milligrams per liter on four hundred milligrams daily in her In Class Practice. She said, Don't panic if I ask you to round to the nearest ten. Concept items ask what R means, how long steady state takes, and what a small dose increase near saturation does: a disproportionately large rise in C s s. Her sheets also ask the half life and the clearance at the target level, or at each dose's own steady state level, as in objective two.

card.m: dose for C<sub>ss</sub> 15 mg/L → C<sub>ss</sub> at another dose (400 mg/day → 11.5 mg/L)
small dose ↑ near saturation → large C<sub>ss</sub> ↑
